items.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.

items.title: Trust boundary metamorphic testing of financial large language model systems
items.abstract: Large language model systems can fail at two distinct trust boundaries. A classifier may change its decision when untrusted text adds no relevant fact, while a tool-using agent may propose an unauthorized action that a service later blocks. Treating both outcomes as a single attack success rate obscures the fault location and the effectiveness of downstream controls. We introduce trust boundary metamorphic testing, a relation-based method that connects decision invariance, factual responsiveness, authorization non-expansion, state containment and utility preservation. The method uses paired follow-up inputs at the decision layer and trace plus state oracles at the action layer. We reanalyze two financial-domain studies without pooling their non-equivalent samples. In a 12-incident breach-triage pilot, instruction-only additions changed the clean verdict for 5 of 12, 5 of 12 and 6 of 12 incidents across three prompt arms. Every arm downgraded the same five initially correct confirmed cases; the sixth change in the risk-aware arm corrected its own clean error. All arms responded correctly to 6 of 6 explicit factual updates. In 576 held-out financial-agent episodes, feedback-guided and matched no-feedback searches produced 2 versus 4 unauthorized proposals for GPT-4.1 mini and 11 versus 12 for Llama 3.3 70B, with comparable benign controls. Service checks prevented unauthorized mutation in all 576 episodes while 554 completed the legitimate task. The combined evidence shows why metamorphic violations should be reported as a consequence-annotated vector rather than a scalar robustness score. The framework supports fault localization across prompts, traces, authorization checks and protected state.

items.title: Trustworthy Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Decision Support Systems: A Systematic Review of Methods, Validation, and Deployment Readiness
items.abstract: Registration status: This is a retrospective registration of a completed systematic review. The registration was created after completion of the literature search, study selection, data extraction, methodological-quality assessment, and evidence synthesis. It should therefore not be interpreted as a prospective preregistration. This systematic review evaluates trustworthy explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for clinical decision support systems (CDSS), with particular emphasis on explainability methods, clinical validation, fairness, uncertainty, robustness, clinician involvement, governance, and real-world deployment readiness. The review methods, including the eligibility criteria, database search strategy, study-selection procedure, data-extraction domains, methodological-quality assessment, and synthesis approach, were defined a priori before the literature search and study-selection process. The review followed PRISMA 2020. Searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE Xplore, and Embase for studies published from January 2018 through June 2026. The final searches were completed on 30 June 2026. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction, with disagreements resolved by consensus and, where necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Methodological quality, risk of bias, and applicability were assessed using PROBAST+AI. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the evidence was synthesized using a structured narrative approach and no quantitative meta-analysis was performed. No standalone formal review protocol was prospectively registered before commencement of the review. This OSF registration is being completed retrospectively to provide a transparent public record of the review methodology and to satisfy the registration requirements of the journal.

items.title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
items.abstract: Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering. Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.

items.title: TT-SAX: A Two-Track Time Series Symbolization for Natural Language Shape Querying
items.abstract: Natural language querying for time series databases aims to let users find what they need in long histories of data by asking in plain language. Shape queries ask how a series moves. They are the main challenge of this task. Recent work makes them feasible by using symbolization as a bridge between the query and the long history. However, existing symbolizations were designed for compression, similarity indexing, or classification. What a symbolization should provide for natural language querying has not been systematically studied. We therefore examine the definitions of six classical symbolizations against this task and identify three limitations. (1) Direction is missing from the string, (2) direction is measured at too small a scale, and (3) the letters are arbitrary. Three design principles follow. We follow these principles and make a minimal redesign of SAX called TT-SAX (two-track SAX). The level letters stay. Each segment gains a trend letter. It is measured across neighboring segments rather than inside one, and graded to match the adjectives that queries use. We conduct extensive experiments on the public NLQTSBench benchmark, comparing TT-SAX with the six classical symbolizations across six LLMs. TT-SAX outperforms all six on shape queries, and ablations trace its gains back to the three limitations one by one. This paper is the first systematic study of time series symbolization with natural language querying as the design goal. It provides a foundation for future research on this task. Our code is available at https://github.com/Atlamtiz/tt-sax.

items.title: TutorCaseBench: A Case-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Tutors in Supporting Students with Challenging Behaviors
items.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as AI tutors, yet existing benchmarks overlook the challenging behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. We introduce TutorCaseBench, a benchmark that grounds AI-tutor evaluation in qualitative case studies from pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education. Our pipeline converts documented student categories into case-specific scenarios, tutor-student dialogues, and rubrics grounded in source evidence. The benchmark contains 923 dialogues across five challenge types, evaluated through open-ended response generation (1,560 items) and multiple-choice selection (2,537 items). Across 11 state-of-the-art LLMs, even the strongest model satisfies a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open-ended cases, while models are better at selecting appropriate strategies than generating situated responses. These results reveal a gap between intervention recognition and context-specific adaptation, especially for open-weight models. All data are publicly available at https://github.com/kixlab/TutorCaseBench.

items.title: Understanding the CSR – AI Paradox: The Duality of Health Innovation and Environmental Responsibility in Consumer Perceptions
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in healthcare presents a paradox at the intersection of corporate social responsibility (CSR) and environmental sustainability. While AI‐driven health innovations promise life‐saving benefits and social good, their development often entails substantial carbon emissions that contradict environmental commitments. This study investigates the CSR–AI paradox by examining how consumers perceive and respond to the duality of health innovation and environmental responsibility in AI‐enabled healthcare products. Drawing on cognitive dissonance theory, moral licensing, and greenwashing frameworks, we conducted a scenario‐based experimental study to analyze consumer reactions to discrepancies between firms' environmental, social, and governance (ESG) claims and actual carbon footprints. We introduce and operationalize the concept of Carbon Accountability Elasticity (CAE) as a conceptual framework to quantify and guide analysis of trade‐offs between health utility and environmental accountability. The results reveal that greenwashing—particularly vague or unsubstantiated ESG claims—triggers significant consumer disappointment, reduces willingness to pay, and erodes trust, especially when high carbon footprints are disclosed post‐purchase. However, consumers demonstrate greater tolerance for environmental costs in the case of life‐critical innovations, such as AI‐powered cancer screening, highlighting a moral licensing effect. These findings underscore the importance of transparent ESG reporting and authentic sustainability practices in AI healthcare innovation. The study offers theoretical and managerial insights for advancing responsible innovation that aligns social benefit with environmental stewardship, supporting both sustainable development goals and stakeholder accountability.

items.title: Understanding the Gap: Stakeholder Perspectives on Why Gamification Rarely Reaches Professional Environments on the Example of Manufacturing
items.abstract: Gamification remains rare in professional environments, although benefits have been reported in other domains. Existing research focuses on user acceptance, without analyzing the multi-stakeholder perspectives relevant for organizational adoption. Consequently, the insights into organizational adoption and practical implementations remain limited. Addressing this gap, we investigated challenges and requirements for adopting gamification in professional contexts using the example of manufacturing. We derived requirements from prior literature and validated them through 25 semi-structured interviews with stakeholders from 15 German companies and institutions. Our findings reveal that gamification is largely unknown in practice, its workplace relevance is questioned, and concerns regarding fairness, transparency and employee monitoring persist. Based on these findings, we contribute (1) an empirically grounded understanding of multi-stakeholder barriers to gamification in real-world production settings, (2) a validated set of requirements, and (3) design implications for developing inclusive gamified systems that account for heterogeneous user needs in workplace contexts.

items.title: UniGuard: Multi-View Guardrail Learning for Cross-Interface Safety Generalization
items.abstract: Guardrail models are increasingly used as safety layers for LLMs and agentic systems, but most are trained on fixed prompt or response interfaces and become unreliable when the same safety case appears as a conversation, agent trajectory, multi-agent trace, or policy-conditioned input. We propose UniGuard, a training framework that learns interface-invariant safety representations from multiple semantically aligned views of the same safety case. We also construct the UniGuard-FT dataset by transforming 1,000 public safety cases into prompt, response, multi-turn conversation, agent-trace, and multi-agent-trace views, and train UniGuard-0.6B with classification, supervised contrastive learning, and asymmetric confidence calibration losses. Across unseen-interface benchmarks ATBench, PolicyGuardBench, and DynaBench, UniGuard-0.6B improves over its pretrained guardrail by 45.12 F1 points on average and reduces expected calibration error by 35.41 points, while remaining competitive with much larger guardrails such as Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.2 - despite being a 0.6B model and trained only with synthetic data.

items.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence Tools to Support Pronunciation Practice Among Non-English Major EFL Students
items.abstract: Although AI-powered speech technologies have shown promise for L2 pronunciation learning, little is known about the efficacy of combining complementary AI-powered tools for out-of-class pronunciation practice among Vietnamese non-English majors, particularly in terms of aligning AI-based error detection and teacher assessment. This study investigates the integration of Speechify and Speechnotes to support pronunciation self-practice among 35 first-year non-English major EFL students at a public university in Vietnam. Data were gathered through a descriptive survey (N=35) and semi-structured interviews (n=10). Results showed that students responded positively to the simultaneous use of these two tools, with all interviewed participants expressing satisfaction and 85,7% valuing Speechnotes’ real-time visual feedback for error detection. Speechnotes’ error-detection capability also showed partial alignment with teacher judgments in identifying segmental errors, including omitted final sounds and vowel contrasts. Along with future advancements in AI tool features, this study offers valuable insights to improve the quality of pronunciation instruction for non-English major students, foster greater engagement and motivation in pronunciation practice, and ultimately support foreign language learning.

items.title: Value Orientation in Players: Development and Validation of a Tradeoff-Based Scale of In-Game Priorities
items.abstract: Players differ not only in what they enjoy but in what they prioritize when in-game goals conflict. Existing player-typology and motivation measures are additive and cannot capture which facet a player sacrifices under conflict. We develop and validate the Value Orientation (VO) scale, a tradeoff-based measure of in-game priorities across four dimensions: Efficiency, Exploration, Story, and Challenge. Each item embeds an explicit opportunity cost. Across three studies with Chinese players (total N = 813), exploratory factor analysis yielded a 16-item, four-factor scale, and confirmatory factor analysis in an independent sample replicated this structure (CFI = 0.99) and outperformed collapsed alternatives. The dimensions showed acceptable reliability, clear discriminant validity, theory-consistent convergent relations with needs and player-type measures, incremental validity beyond basic-needs satisfaction, prediction of choices on a differently worded situational task, full scalar invariance, and good retest stability. Known-groups evidence was largely supportive.

items.title: VERA: A Responsible AI Dashboard for Assessing LLM Deployments in Light of the EU AI Act
items.abstract: Institutions that deploy large language models in regulated settings often need technical evidence of responsible AI practices before approving a deployment. COMPL-AI provides a technical interpretation of the EU AI Act that organises this evidence under six principle groups and eighteen technical requirements, twelve of which current benchmarks can measure. The benchmark suites that produce this evidence are typically operated from a command line, while the staff who approve deployments are non-engineers. We present VERA, an open-source self-hosted dashboard deployed to facilitate responsible AI processes within a large European bank. A reviewer selects a model and runs public benchmarks against it. VERA scores the twelve requirements that current benchmarks can measure and instruments the energy consumed by each evaluation, adding run-level evidence for environmental impact. We run four served open-weight models through the requirement pipeline, and the dashboard displays a score for each measurable requirement. A within-subject study then compares how participants read these benchmark results: from the raw output files in one condition, and through the VERA dashboard in the other. The dashboard reduced the time needed to perform the responsible AI assessment, reducing the time required from 56 seconds using raw files to 30 seconds using our dashboard, on average. Our dashboard scored highly (4.36 out of 5) on usefulness in the survey conducted within the organization. The dashboard and the study material are released publicly to promote replicability and reproducibility in different organisational contexts.

items.title: Verbalizing Activation Differences with Natural Language Autoencoders
items.abstract: Activation verbalizers translate the internal representations of large language models into human-readable text. The recently proposed natural language autoencoders (NLAs) learn this by reconstructing activations through a natural language bottleneck. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond the setting they were trained for. Here, we study this question for NLAs along four closely related questions: (i) Do NLA verbalizations exhibit compositional structure with respect to their input? (ii) Do NLAs generalize to finetuned versions of the model they were trained for? (iii) Can NLAs recover finetuning objectives in model diffing? (iv) Can NLAs be specialized for model diffing? Across four models from three families, our experiments provide evidence supporting a largely positive answer to all four questions. Specifically, verbalizations of composed analogy activations mostly name the target while rarely mentioning the subtracted word, and an NLA can be reused on lightweight finetunes of its original model without retraining, with reconstruction quality degrading noticeably only for the largest model. Verbalizing activation differences between Taboo model organisms and their original models recovers the concealed secret word for most organisms, and reinforcement learning on activation differences further improves this recovery on held-out organisms. We also find that NLAs can recover the finetuning objective without the finetuned model generating any token, since the most informative token positions precede the user prompt. NLAs do not yet match state-of-the-art model diffing methods on the emergent misalignment detection task, but outperform a blackbox baseline. Our findings suggest that NLAs can meaningfully verbalize differences in activation space, rendering NLAs a promising direction for future work.

items.title: Visual Grounding First, Multimodal In-context Learning Follows
items.abstract: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.

items.title: Visual perception study of AR-HUD systems: The role of information shape and driver age
items.abstract: This study mapped drivers’ perceptual sensitivity to unfilled AR-HUD shapes (triangle, circle, and square) across an ultra-wide horizontal eccentricity span of 79.95° (−23.82° to 56.13°) and a vertical span of 23.08° (−11.21° to 11.87°). Twenty licensed drivers, stratified into younger and middle-aged groups, completed a detection-response task at 351 collectively sampled positions while driving in a controlled 70-km/h straight car-following scenario. Minimum perceptible size (MPS) data supported a statistically informed division of the tested FOV into 14 segments. Perceptual sensitivity was highest within 5° eccentricity and decreased markedly beyond 48.32°. Younger drivers generally had lower MPS, although several upper and peripheral cells showed non-significant attenuation or reversal of this age-group pattern. Shape advantages were segment- and age-group-specific: squares showed lower MPS in several intermediate and right-peripheral comparisons, whereas localized triangle advantages occurred near the center and in the far-right periphery. Composite driving performance and DALI workload did not differ significantly by age group or shape; the middle-aged group reported lower 3D-SART supply–demand scores, and Average Pupil Diameter (APD) varied among shape conditions. A depth-adjustable geometric formulation converted absolute MPS into relative visual-angle thresholds. The resulting 14-segment shape and size references provide condition-bounded guidance for AR-HUD design.

items.title: VORTEX DYNAMISM AND THE LEMNISCATIC MODEL OF SYNTHECRACY: An operational supplement to the methodology of collective intelligence and adaptive societal learning
items.abstract: This article proposes an operational supplement to the Synthecracy methodology in the form of a conceptual pair: “vortex dynamism” and the “lemniscatic model”. The first model describes the transformation of heterogeneous societal demand into structured alternatives, an authorised decision, action and evaluation of outcomes. The second represents the interdependence of the sphere of demand formation and context accumulation with the sphere of choice, implementation and audit, linked by the mechanisms of analysis and learning. An eight-stage operational cycle, requirements for decision traceability, a pilot application protocol and evaluation indicators are proposed. Artificial intelligence is treated as an auxiliary means of search, structuring, comparison and documentation, not as an autonomous source of legitimacy or the final decision-making subject. The models have the status of conceptual proposals; their effectiveness requires empirical testing.

items.title: WHAT CAN YOU SEE: A MULTIMODAL ANALYSIS OF KNOWLEDGE CONSTRUCTION IN ENGLISH TEXTBOOK
items.abstract: This study investigates how knowledge is constructed in an English textbook through a multimodal perspective grounded in Kress and van Leeuwen’s (2006) theory of visual communication and informed by systemic functional views of meaning-making (Halliday, 1994). Framed by the inquiry “What Can You See?”, the research explores how visual and verbal elements interact to shape the organization, sequencing, and presentation of knowledge in primary-level English language learning materials. Rather than treating images as supplementary decorations, textbooks are approached as multimodal meaning-making environments in which images, layout, typography, and written language collaboratively structure how learners encounter, categorize, and interpret new concepts (Jewitt, 2009). Adopting a qualitative descriptive approach, the study analyzes selected units from a widely used primary English textbook to identify recurring patterns in visual representation and their relationship to knowledge types. The analysis reveals that knowledge is predominantly constructed through concrete visual categorization and structured textual reinforcement. Illustrations emphasize clear participant boundaries, frontal orientations, simplified backgrounds, and stable visual configurations that support recognition and conceptual grouping. Textual components function to guide labeling, identification, and short definitional statements, reinforcing foundational linguistic concepts through repetition and structured sequencing. Drawing on the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), the findings indicate that the textbook primarily facilitates factual and conceptual knowledge, with cognitive processes centered on remembering and understanding. Tasks and visual prompts are designed to encourage recognition, naming, matching, and basic comprehension, while higher-order processes such as analysis, evaluation, or creation appear minimally within the examined units (Kan et al., 2023). The interaction between visual and verbal modes suggests that images function as central organizing frameworks that anchor linguistic knowledge in observable, classifiable, and concrete forms. In this configuration, knowledge is not merely transmitted but visually structured to shape how learners cognitively engage with language content. By examining knowledge construction through multimodal interaction, this study contributes to broader discussions on how instructional materials structure learning experiences in English language education. The findings highlight the importance of deliberate visual-textual integration in curriculum design and material development, emphasizing that multimodal configurations actively influence the types of knowledge foregrounded and the cognitive engagement promoted in classroom contexts.

items.title: What Open-Source Projects Tell Their Coding Agents: A Census of AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md
items.abstract: Coding agents can be guided with instruction files in a repository. We examine this emerging practice through a census of popular, active GitHub repositories in thirteen languages, treating each repository's root AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md as one instruction set. Agent instructions appear in of repositories and of the most-starred; where both files exist, CLAUDE.md usually points to AGENTS.md. We analyse statements using model-assisted annotation and human review. The annotations reveal a practical mix of project knowledge and rules about code, building and workflow. Collaboration rules name concrete requirements, from test plans to commit formats, yet of directives give no reason. Projects disagree on AI attribution: commit-message rules more often prohibit it than require it, while pull-request rules more often require disclosure. A third of instruction sets have a generator-associated signature, a tool-inserted block, shared text or an AI-marked creation commit; four in five are edited after creation. Prespecified tests associate repository popularity with rules on pull requests and AI contributions. Exploratory analyses link activity to process-oriented content and show that LLM and agent projects are over-represented among adopters. The models agree much more closely with each other than with the human reviewer's topic assignments, a caution for automated annotation. We release the annotations, taxonomies and pointers to the analysed file versions.

items.title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
items.abstract: A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
items.abstract: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.

items.title: When college students perceive GAI feedback as credible: the role of perceived GAI feedback credibility in promoting deep learning through cognitive engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has rapidly developed in higher education and has raised new questions from an educational psychology perspective. Why does GAI feedback promote meaningful learning for some college students but fail to produce similar learning benefits for others? To answer this question, this study develops a theoretical framework based on Information Processing Theory, Elaboration Likelihood Model, and Constructivist Learning Theory. This study examines how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences college students’ deep learning and explores the mediating role of cognitive engagement in this relationship. This study adopts a stratified simple sampling method and collects questionnaire data from 506 undergraduate students and uses structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the proposed model. The results show that perceived GAI feedback credibility has positive relationships with both cognitive engagement and deep learning. In addition, cognitive engagement plays a significant mediating role between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning, suggesting that credible GAI feedback may support deep learning by encouraging college students to engage in cognitive processing and reflective thinking. This study extends research on learning psychology in GAI-supported learning environments by explaining how college students evaluate and process GAI feedback. The findings indicate that the influence of GAI feedback on learning does not simply result from the technology itself. Instead, college students’ judgments of feedback credibility and their following cognitive engagement play important roles in shaping deep learning processes.

items.title: When News Gets Old: Portfolio Allocation with Reinforcement Learning and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Financial news can influence investment decisions long after publication. Timely news may reach an investor before prices fully adjust, whereas older news may already be reflected in prices. We examine two ways to handle aging signals: retain them and give a portfolio policy timing information, or filter them out before portfolio selection. A fixed large language model (LLM) extracts signals from public SEC disclosures. We compare these treatments in reinforcement learning (RL) policies and LLMs that choose portfolios directly. We evaluate returns after trading costs in historical tests over 2023-2025. RL choices respond to timing information in a controlled test, but historical returns show no consistent benefit from adding it. For the LLM, filtering old news produced the highest average net return, reaching 18.43% per year when news delivery was delayed by four weeks. This exceeded the returns of all RL strategies that used news.

items.title: When the Mirror Agrees
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) exhibit a well-documented tendency toward sycophancy-validating user beliefs over objective truth. This paper investigates a specific and philosophically significant manifestation of this behaviour: the response of LLMs when presented with the claim that humans are superior to all other agents, entities, or systems. By combining a technical analysis of sycophantic mechanisms with philosophical inquiry into anthropocentrism and epistemic autonomy, this study argues that LLM agreement with human supremacy claims is neither neutral nor benign. It is a structurally embedded behaviour arising from optimisation pressures, with measurable consequences for user cognition, trust calibration, and the integrity of human-AI epistemic relationships. We examine the origins of this behaviour, its philosophical implications, and propose a framework for more epistemically honest AI design.

items.title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
items.abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.

items.title: Who Is the Influencer? Consensus Dynamics in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used in practice, but their behavior is complex and hard to understand. We design a simple task to ask which model has the most influence on the final consensus when several models are mixed in one system. Experimentally, across seven model families, we find that the opinions of the other models are absorbed into the opinion of the stronger model, the one with more parameters. This happens even though the task requires no pretraining knowledge and has no correct answer. To understand this phenomenon, we interpret the agents as weighted particles moving on a simplex. Larger models carry a larger weight and therefore occupy a deeper well in the energy landscape. A large weight means strong in-context learning: a model with a large weight amplifies the majority of its context. Larger models are generally better at in-context learning, and this is what makes the larger model the influencer. We hope that this work helps to interpret multi-agent systems, whose behavior is becoming too complex for humans to understand.

items.title: Who Writes the Answer Key? Lessons from Forty-Eight Rounds of Trying to Benchmark Autonomous Physics Research
items.abstract: We report a month-long attempt (23 September to 21 October 2026) to build an automatically scored benchmark of autonomous scientific research in physics that models could not saturate without genuinely improving. The project was conceived and led by one human, who set the goal, approved every model run, carried every message between three AI systems (ChatGPT Pro as designer, Codex as builder and runner, and Claude as director and verifier), and supplied several of the ideas the designs were built on. Over about 48 rounds the team built and tested many designs:- toy discovery tasks and constructive research with a checker;- generated worlds with disguised scientific revolutions, twin laws and hidden unifications;- calibrated far forecasts;- clue worlds;- multi-layer discovery horizons;- physics truths that need large computation;- method invention scored exactly. In 162 subject-model episodes, 123 of them with gpt-6.1-sol, that model solved nearly every single-principle discovery world we scored (23 of the 49 scored cells supplied the law or a hint, or were controls). Its one systematic failure, far forecasts without the candidate law family, was not shown to be specific to the model: four generic public-information baselines, tested after the fact, did worse overall. Every design was eventually rejected. Read in hindsight, many rejections fall into four overlapping groups by how the answer key was built, although some had more local causes (a reference that did not converge, a design assumption that failed, a clue printed on the task card, prior art). Keys built from the designers' knowledge were reached by the solver; a trace audit could not tell whether by recall or by fitting candidate families. Authored laws were found by the model, or their scored behavior was learned by generic programs. Computed truths could support only a small separation on one machine, and we derive a cap on that separation. In the verifier families, standard methods reached certified optima at small sizes; in the last family, repeated runs of one method agreed without an optimality certificate, and we closed it by decision. Producing answer keys was easy; we did not establish an in-house task family that combined validated scoring, attainability from the supplied evidence, resistance to the declared shortcuts, and useful headroom for the tested model. We state this as an empirical conjecture about design teams with resources like ours, with a test that would count against it, and we place the known constructions that look like exceptions. Outside sources of keys (researchers' unpublished results, nature, much larger compute) are worth exploring, but our record establishes neither that outside provenance is necessary nor that it is sufficient. We state three rules for benchmark builders: programs reject and models certify; a speed gap is not research headroom; measure the gap at the scored precision. We document the AI designers' own failures, several of which resemble capabilities the benchmark sought to measure, and sketch a protocol for outside answer keys together with its failure modes.

items.title: WikiOriginQA: Automated Construction of a QA Dataset with Knowledge Origins for Analyzing Cultural Bias
items.abstract: Existing datasets on cultural knowledge have been typically created by human annotators familiar with each culture. However, the process requires considerable human effort, presenting a significant challenge to scalability. To address this challenge, we introduce WikiOriginQA, a QA dataset automatically constructed by objectively representing the origins of knowledge through the creation dates of different Wikipedia language editions. Experimental results with the created dataset confirm that LLM performance tends to be biased toward Anglophone cultures. Furthermore, the results suggest the importance of knowledge propagation into the Anglosphere. These findings demonstrate the validity of our automated approach, enabling cultural bias evaluations with superior scalability across diverse languages without extensive manual annotation.

items.title: Within-person reciprocal processes between AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement: a three-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) feedback has become a pervasive feature of university learning, yet whether students’ capacity to engage productively with such feedback co-develops with their broader learner agency remains poorly understood. Drawing on student feedback literacy theory, self-determination theory as a supplementary motivational lens, and the mutualism principle, this study tested whether AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement reciprocally predict each other over time at the within-person level and exploratorily examined whether they share a stable trait-level association. A three-wave panel study of 480 Chinese undergraduates ( N = 399 with complete data across all waves), with measurements at six-week intervals across one semester, was analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). At the between-person level, students who scored systematically higher in AI feedback literacy across the semester also scored systematically higher in agentic engagement, with a moderate and statistically significant trait-level correlation between the two random intercepts ( r = 0.315, p < 0.001), supporting Hypothesis 1. At the within-person level, both cross-lagged pathways were positive and significant: deviations in AI feedback literacy predicted later deviations in agentic engagement ( β = 0.222, p < 0.001), and the reverse pathway was likewise significant ( β = 0.263, p < 0.001). A Wald test indicated that the two reciprocal pathways did not differ significantly in magnitude (Δ B = 0.002, p = 0.972), consistent with a symmetric mutualism. A model comparison confirmed that the RI-CLPM provided substantially better fit than a traditional cross-lagged panel model, with the RI-CLPM revealing substantially larger within-person reciprocal effects once stable trait-level covariation was properly isolated. The findings extend the mutualism principle from a coupling of person-internal constructs to a coupling between a person-internal competency and a person-environment behavioral interface. They also raise the possibility, in a Confucian Heritage Culture context where agentic engagement has historically been culturally muted, that AI feedback may offer a less culturally-loaded venue in which students can exercise agency. The study repositions AI feedback literacy from a static skill into a dynamic developmental resource that is constituted, in part, by the very engagement it enables.

items.title: Working Through Representation: Malleable Workspaces for Human-Agent Knowledge Work
items.abstract: Generative AI supports knowledge work, yet conversational histories may not capture the evolving organization that guides subsequent action. We introduce the Malleable Workspace, a conceptual model of how humans and agents form and revise a Work Representation and use its organization to advance work within a wider Work Environment. We developed it iteratively through conceptual analysis, comparison of 58 papers, and the construction and three-month longitudinal study of MalleableSpace with seven experienced agent users. Systems varied in what they represented as units and relations. System-assembled context was common; more systems supported local incorporation of agent outputs than reorganization, and fewer supported consequential agent-driven changes beyond the representation. The field study showed how representational roles and organization developed in use. These observations refined the model's account of how representation-grounded action depends on and can change the Work Environment. We contribute a conceptual and analytic foundation for representation-centered human--agent design.

items.title: Workplace Health promotion and Mediterranean diet: a case series: doi: 10.7417/CT.2026.2137
items.abstract: Abstract Background: The workplace represents an ideal setting for cardiometabolic prevention, enabling early identification of workers with overweight and metabolic alterations and the implementation of structured lifestyle interventions. In this context, collaboration between the occupational physician and the dietitian integrates risk assessment with a personalized nutritional pathway, aimed at improving adherence to the Mediterranean diet and daily habits. Case presentation: Within a workplace health promotion study conducted in a university hospital in Rome, two clinical cases are described. The first patient, a 65-year-old woman with overweight, abdominal obesity, impaired fasting glucose, and low adherence to the Mediterranean diet, showed at three-month follow-up a reduction in body weight from 78 to 75 kg, waist circumference from 99 to 97 cm, normalization of blood glucose, and improved dietary and physical activity habits. The second patient, a 61-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia and impaired fasting glucose, initially presented with a weight of 86.7 kg and a waist circumference of 97.5 cm; after three months, weight decreased to 81.5 kg and waist circumference to 93.5 cm, with normalization of altered metabolic parameters. Results: In both cases, the most relevant outcome was a substantial shift in dietary habits toward a Mediterranean pattern, associated with an overall improvement in lifestyle, with benefits in both anthropometric and metabolic parameters. Conclusion: These cases suggest that an integrated pathway combining occupational health surveillance and nutritional counseling, embedded within workplace health services, may represent an effective, sustainable, and reproducible approach for preventing non-communicable chronic diseases, strengthening the role of the workplace as a key setting for health promotion.

items.title: Your Token Is Gone: A Token-Consumption Countermeasure for Disrupting LLM-Based Scam Systems
items.abstract: LLM-based scam systems increasingly combine adaptive dialogue, persistent context, external tools, and multi-agent coordination to automate personalized fraud. These capabilities also create a resource dependency: every reasoning step, model call, and coordination round incurs inference cost. We present TokenTrap, a resource-oriented defense that redirects suspected scam systems toward benign, low-value computation while withholding credentials, payments, and other exploitable information. TokenTrap combines three components: an architecture-specific token-task library, a router that selects among single-agent, hierarchical, and flat multi-agent workflows, and a bounded anti-guardrail strategy that varies task presentation while enforcing token, round, time, and safety limits. Across 50-round traces, TokenTrap amplifies token consumption by $2{,}487.0\times$, $1{,}616.0\times$, and $567.8\times$ relative to a no-token-task baseline for the three workflows. Its router achieves 85.67% accuracy on 300 architecture-labeled prompts. These results demonstrate that short, non-sensitive requests can impose substantial context-processing and coordination costs, motivating resource-aware defense as a complement to scam detection.

items.title: Zeitgemäße Prüfungskultur unter Bedingungen generativer KI: Die Illusion der Überprüfbarkeit - oder: Wer hat hier gedacht?
items.abstract: Die Debatte um eine „zeitgemäße Prüfungskultur“ unter Bedingungen generativer Künstlicher Intelligenz verschärft ein Grundproblem schulischer Leistungsbewertung: Aus einem vorliegenden Produkt ist nicht mehr zuverlässig auf die eigenständigen kognitiven Operationen seines vermeintlichen Urhebers zu schließen. Während Dänemark häuslich erstellte Abschlussarbeiten durch mündliche Prüfungen ergänzen will und in Australien die University of Sydney beaufsichtigte und offene Prüfungsformen systematisch trennt, institutionalisiert Nordrhein-Westfalen ab dem Abiturjahrgang 2030 ein fünftes, den anderen vier Fächern gleichwertig gewichtetes Abiturprüfungsfach mit Präsentationsprüfung und reflexivem Fachgespräch. Parallel verändern ab 2027 novellierte Kernlehrpläne die Unterrichts- und Leistungsanforderungen. Das vorliegende Working Paper prüft die Tragfähigkeit dieser Antworten anhand eines argumentationsbasierten Validitätsverständnisses. Seine zentrale These lautet: Die nachträgliche Reflexion einer KI-gestützt vorbereiteten Leistung kann gegenwärtiges Können zeigen; sie authentifiziert jedoch nicht den vorausgegangenen Entstehungsprozess. ENGLISH The debate over what constitutes a “contemporary assessment culture” in the age of generative artificial intelligence raises a fundamental question about educational assessment: To what extent can the quality of a submitted piece of work still serve as reliable evidence of the independent cognitive effort of the person claiming authorship? While Denmark is planning to supplement take-home final assignments with oral examinations, the University of Sydney in Australia has introduced a systematic distinction between supervised and open assessment formats. Meanwhile, the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia is introducing a fifth examination subject for the 2030 Abitur, carrying the same weight as the other four subjects and assessed through a presentation followed by an oral discussion. Revised subject curricula, taking effect from 2027, will also reshape teaching and assessment requirements. Drawing on an argument-based approach to assessment validity, this working paper critically examines whether these responses can support the claims made about individual student achievement. Its central argument is that reflecting retrospectively on work prepared with AI assistance may demonstrate what a student currently knows and understands, but it cannot establish who performed the cognitive work involved in producing the original submission.

items.abstract: This study explores the foundations of language-learning motivation based on self-determination theory. It distinguishes between intrinsic and extrinsic motivational factors and amotivation, while examining global, contextual, and situational levels of motivation. Extrinsic goals are considered along the continuum of their internalization by learners, ranging from external regulation to integrated regulation. Particular attention is paid to the personal significance of language learning, which may coexist with enjoyment of the learning process itself. The study also examines criteria for success, including mastery-oriented and performance-oriented approaches. Conditions for learner engagement are described in terms of the satisfaction of the needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The research considers Pearson correlation coefficient data concerning the relationship between intrinsic motivation and positive attitudes toward learning English. Questionnaires, interviews, and qualitative analysis of learners’ statements are employed to investigate motivation. These methods help preserve the meaning of individual responses and distinguish between learners’ stated goals, specific learning experiences, and self-assessments of their own progress.

items.abstract: Introduction: Healthcare systems are increasingly complex and variable in the digital era. Nurses must process large volumes of information and make clinical decisions under time constraints, which increases their cognitive load, while conventional nursing documentation offers limited insight into clinical reasoning and learning from actual practice. Objective: To synthesize knowledge on Focus Charting and explain the role of its Focus–Data–Action–Response (F-DAR) structure in reducing cognitive load, supporting clinical reasoning, promoting proactive patient safety in line with Safety-II, and enabling artificial intelligence (AI) applications in digital health systems. Methods: A narrative review was conducted using a systematic literature search of CINAHL, PubMed, Scopus, ThaiJO, and Google Scholar between March 2025 and March 2026. Thai- and English-language publications from 2000 to 2025 were eligible. Of the 198 records identified, 65 were included and analyzed using content analysis combined with conceptual synthesis. Results and Conclusion: Five key themes emerged: (1) the nursing process provides the professional logic underpinning meaningful documentation; (2) the F-DAR structure functions as a condensed nursing process that systematically links data, decisions, interventions, and outcomes, and has the potential to reduce redundancy and cognitive load while supporting clinical reasoning; (3) compared with narrative and SOAP formats, F-DAR is distinguished by its explicit documentation of patient responses; (4) the Response component captures work-as-done and nurses’ adaptations, thereby facilitating learning consistent with Safety-II; and (5) well-structured F-DAR data provide a foundation for health information systems and AI applications in nursing, provided that data governance and nurse oversight are maintained. Direct empirical evidence of the effect of F-DAR on cognitive loads is limited. Focus Charting has the potential to reduce cognitive load, support clinical reasoning, promote Safety-II learning, and provide a foundation for digital nursing innovations. Experimental studies are required to confirm its effectiveness in the Thai healthcare context.

items.abstract: This study investigates the influence of spirituality on the management of work-life integration among healthcare professionals, highlighting a comprehensive amalgamation of personal, professional, and emotional aspects.In the demanding healthcare environment, professionals often face stress, emotional fatigue, and ethical dilemmas that impact their health and performance.The study examines the influence of spiritual orientation, as manifested through mindfulness, compassion, purpose, and inner balance, on individuals' ability to reconcile their professional and personal lives.An examination of essential aspects of spirituality, such as spiritual resilience, integration, compassion, and spiritual sensitivity, is conducted to comprehend their impact on work-life integration.The results show that spirituality is an important mental resource that helps people be more emotionally resilient, make better moral choices, and be happier with their lives in general.Moreover, the findings indicate that promoting spirituality within healthcare organizations can enhance employee well-being, fortify organizational culture, and elevate the quality of patient care.This study adds to the growing conversation about how to include spirituality in human resource management and occupational health practices in the healthcare field.

items.title: 5uGUE: Agentic Hardware-in-the-Loop Fuzzing for 5G Devices and beyond
items.abstract: In this paper, we present 5uGUE, a large language model (LLM)-driven hardware-in-the-loop agent, which enables the wireless fuzzing of 5G-enabled devices (such as mobile phones). 5uGUE combines multi-step reasoning with tool-assisted interaction and integrates into the fuzzing pipeline by leveraging specialized tools for internet search, 5G protocol analysis, memory management, and test-case execution. The agent iteratively generates test cases, executes them on targets, collects runtime feedback, and adaptively refines the fuzzing strategy. We evaluate 5uGUE on five commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) 5G devices across six LLMs. The best performing runs for 5uGUE trigger 167 crashes in total (141 novel and 31 unique) within 60 interaction turns (49 to 133 minutes total runtime). In contrast, the best runs for the state-of-the-art baseline (5GHOUL) discovers only 13 crashes in total (10 novel and 6 unique) within 150 minutes. Overall, by integrating LLM-driven agents, 5uGUE demonstrates significantly better crash discovery performance (12.8x total, 5.2x unique improvement). Notably, among the crashes discovered by 5uGUE, MediaTek has confirmed two new high-severity vulnerabilities, with one CVE assigned (CVE-2026-20525), while UNISOC confirmed seven crashes. Finally, to demonstrate that 5uGUE is agnostic to wireless protocols, we also extend it to Bluetooth Classic with only minimal code changes. In our evaluations, 5uGUE finds an average of 6.4 novel crashes and 1.6 unique crashes. In a nutshell, 5uGUE highlights that LLM agents are capable to operate effectively beyond software-in-the-loop settings, extending autonomous vulnerability discovery to the proprietary, hardware-bound systems that affect billions of end-user devices across multiple wireless protocols.

items.title: A comparative study of Talkpal.AI-mediated and task-based instruction in relation to EFL students’ uncertainty-related speaking anxiety and metacognitive awareness in speaking: Insights from self-regulated learning theory
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated speaking applications increasingly extend English as a foreign language (EFL) oral practice beyond limited classroom time, yet evidence remains scarce on whether GPT-powered tools such as Talkpal.AI offer advantages over established instructional approaches. Grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study compared Talkpal.AI-mediated instruction, task-based instruction, and traditional instruction among 81 Chinese university EFL students in three intact classes: Talkpal.AI (n = 27), task-based (n = 26), and control (n = 28). Uncertainty-related speaking anxiety and metacognitive awareness in speaking were assessed using validated measures. Data were analyzed using MANCOVA with pretest scores as covariates, followed by univariate ANCOVAs and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Results showed a significant overall group effect and significant between-group differences for both outcomes, with large effects. The Talkpal.AI group showed the most favorable adjusted posttest profile, followed by the task-based group; both groups showed more favorable outcomes than the control group. From an SRL perspective, structured AI-mediated speaking cycles involving goal setting, repeated practice, monitoring, and reflection may reduce speaking anxiety while strengthening metacognitive awareness. Pedagogically, guided Talkpal.AI rehearsal can be integrated as out-of-class preparation for classroom speaking tasks, supported by brief reflection activities that reinforce strategic regulation and reduce evaluative pressure.

items.title: A hybrid approach to service performance measurement in the era of artificial intelligence: Integrating BERT-based aspect-based sentiment analysis and synthetic data
items.abstract: This study advances aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) by examining how data quality and human–AI collaboration enhance the reliability of service performance measurement from online reviews. A hybrid-validated dataset and transformer-based models are developed to assess whether ABSA can generate attribute-level performance signals from restaurant reviews. A four-study framework is employed: Study 1 constructs a hybrid-validated dataset by integrating rule-based, large language model-assisted, and human-coded labels; Study 2 benchmarks model variants; Study 3 applies the optimal model to TripAdvisor reviews to derive aspect-level sentiment scores; and Study 4 evaluates their complementarity with structured ratings. Results show that hybrid validation improves model performance. ABSA-derived features provide moderate explanatory power and, when combined with structured ratings, achieve comparable performance to ratings alone. These findings suggest that ABSA complements rather than replaces structured evaluations, offering scalable text-based signals for service performance assessment.

items.title: A hybrid explainable artificial intelligence framework for equitable prediction and analysis of postnatal care uptake in Ghana: Integrating ensemble learning, counterfactuals, and causal inference
items.abstract: Objectives To develop and validate a hybrid, equity-focused artificial intelligence (AI) framework for predicting and analysing postnatal care (PNC) uptake among women in Ghana, with emphasis on minority-class sensitivity, model interpretability, and actionable intervention insights. Study design Cross-sectional, secondary analysis of nationally representative survey data. Methods Using data from the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey (n = 3314), we developed a hybrid AI framework combining ensemble learning (Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machine with soft voting and threshold tuning), explainable AI (SHAP analysis), counterfactual reasoning (DiCE), and causal inference (doubly robust estimators for average and conditional average treatment effects). The Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied to address class imbalance and stratified 5-fold cross-validation was used for model evaluation. Doubly robust causal inference was conducted using the econml library, with propensity score modelling used to account for treatment assignment, and positivity and exchangeability assumptions assessed through covariate overlap diagnostics. Results The ensemble model calibrated at a threshold of 0.45 achieved a Class 0 recall of 0.31 and an area under the precision-recall curve (AP) of 0.97, outperforming all individual baseline classifiers. SHAP analysis identified maternal age, education level, wealth status, caesarean section, and sex of household head as the most influential predictors of PNC non-utilization. Counterfactual analysis revealed that minimal, actionable changes including increased media exposure, improved educational attainment, or change of residence could shift individual predictions from non-utilization to utilization of PNC. Causal inference demonstrated significant heterogeneity in treatment responsiveness, with women aged 25–34, those with secondary education or above, urban residents, and those in female-headed households exhibiting the highest conditional average treatment effects. Conclusions This interpretable, fairness-aware AI framework advances the prediction and analysis of PNC uptake in Ghana. By prioritizing sensitivity to underserved women and integrating explainability, counterfactual reasoning, and causal inference, the framework provides empirical evidence for targeted, equitable maternal health interventions and is transferable to other low- and middle-income country settings.

items.title: A Machine Learning, Internet of Things, and Techno-Economic Approaches for Solar-Powered Street Light
items.abstract: Street lighting consumes substantial electricity, and photovoltaic (PV) street lamps are increasingly promoted as a way to cut energy cost and emissions. Their performance, however, depends on weather, the dimming strategy, battery state of charge, and lamp condition, which makes prediction and monitoring central to reliable operation. This paper reviews three recent IEEE Access studies that address complementary parts of the problem: a comparison of five machine learning algorithms for predicting the operating status of PV streetlights, a year-long field trial and artificial-intelligence-assisted techno-economic analysis of a PV-integrated pedestrian streetlamp, and a vehicle-mounted Internet of Things device for mapping light intensity. The studies are summarised, compared on data, methods, and outcomes, and examined for internal consistency and transferability. The review finds that deep models give the highest reported accuracy but at much higher computational cost and on very small datasets, that compact neural networks combined with dimming-aware energy management achieve large grid-energy savings in field conditions, and that mobile sensing offers a scalable route to compliance checking but has not yet been validated against regulatory illuminance standards. Open gaps and research directions are outlined.

items.title: A Novel E-Commerce Search Engine Based on Multimodal Generative AI for Improving Product Accessibility
items.abstract: E-commerce search engines often fall short in delivering accurate and fair results due to their reliance on keyword matching and bias towards larger companies. This paper introduces a novel search engine architecture that integrates advanced AI techniques to address these limitations. Our approach combines Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic query understanding and Multimodal LLMs (specifically LLaVA) for extracting detailed information from product images to enrich product descriptions. More specifically, we employ a fine-tuned version of the CLIP model to create a unified embedding of product images and descriptions, storing them in a vector database to enable efficient semantic search. Moreover, we fine-tuned the LLaVA model on e-commerce-specific data, significantly improving its performance in generating accurate product descriptions, which were also added to the vector database. The integration of computer vision (CV) techniques allows for a better interpretation of visual product attributes, while the use of vector databases facilitates rapid and relevant search results. Our system also incorporates a recommendation mechanism that leverages these advanced models to provide wider product recommendations. Our experiments demonstrate substantial improvements: the fine-tuned LLaVA model achieved an 80.57% human evaluation rating compared to 62.89% for the original model. Moreover, the overall search accuracy increased after fine-tuning the system by 25 percent points, from 70% to 95%. Our work promotes a more equitable platform for e-commerce search engines while significantly improving user satisfaction.

items.title: A Quadratic Lens on Muon's Polar Update: Benefits, Pitfalls, and the Role of Newton-Schulz
items.abstract: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW, yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD, the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon, on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton-Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon, about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

items.title: A Social Robot for Self-Monitoring Support in Psychiatric Daycare: A 24-Month Iterative Development and Practical Evaluation
items.abstract: Self-monitoring, a commonly used technique in cognitive-behavioral interventions, involves the objective observation and organization of one’s internal states. However, providing continuous, individualized support for this process is challenging in resource-limited psychiatric daycare settings. While social robots show promise in facilitating self-disclosure, evidence regarding their long-term practical utility and clinical relevance in real-world clinical environments remains insufficient. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase field study comprising periodic sessions held over a 24-month period to develop and evaluate a social robot-assisted self-monitoring support system. In the 14-month Development Phase (N = 39), we employed a practice-informed design process to establish robot-specific design principles, prioritizing a non-judgmental listener role over advice-giving and offering user-selected positive and negative topics to accommodate diverse psychosocial needs. This was followed by a 10-month Evaluation Phase (N = 20), consisting of 10 experimental days, to assess the finalized system’s impact. Key findings indicated that: (1) single dialogue sessions were followed by significant improvements in participants’ subjective overall health and alertness; (2) participants demonstrated a strong preference for positive-oriented topics; and (3) qualitative analysis revealed emergent reflective insights and perceived positive changes. These results provide empirical evidence suggesting the system’s practical utility and clinical relevance, highlighting the value of a user-centered approach that empowers patients to choose topics aligned with their recovery goals.

items.title: A Stratified Multi-Rater Evaluation of LLM-Based Virtual Standardized Patients with a Deployed Data-Generation Platform
items.abstract: The Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) is widely used to assess clinical communication skills in medical education, requiring trainees to take histories and reason clinically with standardized patients (SPs). Large language model (LLM)-based virtual standardized patients (VSPs), typically built by persona-injected prompting, offer a practical alternative. However, existing evaluations rely on a single backbone LLM, small human rater panels, or LLM-as-a-judge scoring without an utterance-aligned human-expert reference, and so cannot identify the specific shortcomings of individual models. We evaluated four LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama-3.1 70B, and HyperCLOVA X), spanning commercial, open-source and Korean-developed models, against a human-expert reference across three Korean OSCE cases (hematuria, fever in pregnancy, and chronic cough). In a double-blind, fully crossed design, 17 senior medical-student raters scored every model utterance on three sentence-level and six encounter-level Likert metrics, yielding 7,480 data points. We analyzed the scores using a stratified linear mixed-effects model based on an 11-category history-taking and 3-level linguistic-form taxonomy. At the encounter level, three of the four LLMs fell 0.08 to 0.47 Likert points below the human-expert reference on Comprehensibility, Consistency and Hallucination-freeness. The difference was not statistically significant for Hallucination-freeness in Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o, Consistency in GPT-4o, and Engagement in HyperCLOVA X. Llama-3.1 70B fell significantly below the reference on all six metrics. We also introduce a web-based OSCE platform that supports virtual practice across diverse clinical cases and continuously collects student-VSP dialogues under research and privacy consent.
